files.codex/u1-answer-key.json:
{
  "body": "Theme Detectives: 1. Ravi's snow walls keep collapsing because the snow is too fluffy, and he will not accept help. 2. He waves Mina away and says, \"You'll just knock it down.\" 3. He looks at the pile of mush that used to be his wall and realizes his way is not working. 4. At the end he shares the credit and calls it \"Our fort,\" and he grins at his sister. 5. Example themes: Working together can make a hard job possible. Accepting help is not the same as failing. 6. Any detail that shows the change works; strongest: Mina's packed blocks make the fort possible, or \"Our fort.\"\nThe Theme of \"The Kite That Would Not Fly\": Strong themes: Do not give up when something fails the first time; a mistake can be fixed; the people who love us can help us solve problems. Strong details: the kite crashes three times; Lila nearly throws it away; her grandfather says a broken kite and an unfinished kite are not the same; she adds ribbons from her old dress; the kite flies higher than any other.\nTheme Check: Strong themes: You do not have to be the loudest to be important; every part of a team matters; being steady can matter more than being noticed. Noor changes from wanting attention (she picks the biggest drum and plays the loudest) to understanding her role (she keeps a steady beat, the band leans on it, and she is proud though nobody claps). Strong details: \"the drum is not a race\"; her sticks \"hovered above it like birds\"; the band falls apart; \"Not loud. Just steady.\"; \"every note in the room had been standing on her beat.\"\nScoring tip: a response that names a topic (\"drums,\" \"kites\") is Beginning on the theme criterion even if the details are strong; score the evidence criterion on its own.",
  "id": "u1-answer-key",
  "purpose": "answer-key",
  "title": "Answer key: Finding the Theme",
  "visibility": "teacher-only"
}
files.codex/u1-overview.json:
{
  "body": "Theme: the lesson under the story.

A theme is a message the author wants readers to take away, like "Keep trying even when it is hard."

To find a theme, ask:
1. What problem does the main character face?
2. How do they change?
3. What does that teach us about life?

A theme is not the topic. "Kites" is a topic. "Fixing a mistake is better than quitting" is a theme.

This week we read "The Kite That Would Not Fly."",
  "id": "u1-overview",
  "purpose": "context",
  "title": "What Is a Theme?",
  "visibility": "students"
}
files.codex/u1-teacher-guide.json:
{
  "body": "OBJECTIVES
- Students determine a theme of a story from details in the text and summarize the story (RL.4.2).
- Students describe in depth how a main character changes, drawing on specific details (RL.4.3).
- Students refer to details and examples in the text when explaining what it says (RL.4.1).

MATERIALS
- "The Snow Fort" (in the lesson), "The Kite That Would Not Fly" and "The Quiet Drummer" (in the activities), printed or on tablets
- Chart paper with three columns: Problem, Change, Lesson
- Sticky notes for marking details
- A short list of topic words (friendship, mistakes, family) next to sample theme sentences, to show the difference

FIVE-DAY PLAN
Day 1: Read What Is a Theme? together. Sort examples: "kites" and "friendship" are topics; "Fixing a mistake is better than quitting" is a theme. Students turn three topics into theme sentences with a partner.
Day 2: Lesson: Theme Detectives. Read "The Snow Fort" aloud, then fill the Problem, Change, Lesson chart as a class. Students answer the questions on their own.
Day 3: Read "The Kite That Would Not Fly" twice: once for the story, once to mark details on sticky notes. Start the assignment: a theme sentence and two details.
Day 4: Finish the kite response. Partners swap and check: is the first sentence a lesson, not a topic? Does each detail connect to it? Revise.
Day 5: Assessment: Theme Check. Students read "The Quiet Drummer" on their own and write. Read the story aloud to any student whose reading plan allows it; the writing stays their own.

DIFFERENTIATION
- Support: give a theme sentence starter ("The story teaches that when ___, you should ___.") and a two-row organizer for details. Pre-teach march, hover and steady before the assessment.
- Support: let students first say their theme aloud to you, then write it.
- Stretch: ask students to find a second, different theme in the kite story and decide which one the author develops more.
- Multilingual learners: preview each story with pictures and a quick oral retell. Accept a theme sentence in the home language first, then build the English version together. Post the frames from the lesson.

FAMILY NOTE (send home at the start of the unit)
We are learning to find the theme of a story: the lesson underneath it. A topic is one word, like "friendship." A theme is a whole idea, like "Real friends tell you the truth." When you read or watch a story together this week, ask your child: What did the main character learn? What does that teach us? Thank you for reading with us.",
  "id": "u1-teacher-guide",
  "purpose": "context",
  "title": "Teacher guide: Finding the Theme",
  "visibility": "teacher-only"
}
files.codex/u2-answer-key.json:
{
  "body": "Reasons Detective: 1. \"I think our school should plant a garden in the empty space behind the gym.\" 2. A garden is an outdoor classroom; kids who grow vegetables are more likely to try them; it would make the space more beautiful. 3. Measuring bean plants in math, watching a plant's life cycle in science, and the cousin's class charting sunflowers. 4. First, For example, Also, Finally, For all these reasons (any three). 5. \"For all these reasons, a garden would make our school a better place to learn and grow.\" 6. Answers vary; look for a reason named and a sensible idea for stronger evidence (for example, a fact about how many students would use the garden).\nShould Recess Be Longer?: No single answer. A strong piece states the opinion first, gives two or more reasons with an example each (focus after moving, exercise and health, solving problems with friends), uses linking words, and restates the opinion at the end.\nWhich Class Pet Should Room 12 Choose?: Either opinion can earn Advanced. Goldfish facts that support it: quiet, lives 10 years or more, can be left over a weekend with an automatic feeder, students can study water and fish. Guinea pig facts: can be gently held, makes wheeking sounds, students learn to care for it daily. Strong pieces may also use a fact against the other choice (a guinea pig cannot be left alone over a weekend; a goldfish cannot be held).\nScoring tip: on the evidence criterion, a reason supported only by feelings (\"fish are cute\") is Developing; a reason supported by a fact from the sheet is Proficient; a fact that is explained (\"so nobody has to take it home\") is Advanced.",
  "id": "u2-answer-key",
  "purpose": "answer-key",
  "title": "Answer key: Opinion Writing",
  "visibility": "teacher-only"
}
files.codex/u2-overview.json:
{
  "body": "Opinion writing.

An opinion piece has:
- an opinion stated clearly at the start,
- at least two reasons, each with facts or examples,
- linking words like because, for example and also,
- a conclusion that restates your opinion.

A good opinion piece does not just say "I like it." It gives readers reasons that could change their minds.",
  "id": "u2-overview",
  "purpose": "context",
  "title": "Say It and Support It",
  "visibility": "students"
}
files.codex/u2-teacher-guide.json:
{
  "body": "OBJECTIVES
- Students write opinion pieces that state an opinion, give reasons supported by facts and details, link opinion and reasons with words and phrases, and end with a conclusion (W.4.1).
- Students explain how an author uses reasons and evidence to support particular points (RI.4.8).
- Students draw evidence from an informational text to support their writing (W.4.9).

MATERIALS
- "Our School Needs a Garden" (in the lesson) and "Two Class Pets: A Fact Sheet" (in the assessment)
- Highlighters in three colors: opinion, reasons, evidence
- An anchor chart of linking words: because, for example, also, in addition, another reason, for these reasons
- A four-box planner: Opinion, Reason 1 and evidence, Reason 2 and evidence, Conclusion

FIVE-DAY PLAN
Day 1: Read Say It and Support It. Hold a quick "four corners" debate (pizza or tacos?) where students must give a reason, not just a preference. Introduce the planner.
Day 2: Lesson: Reasons Detective. Students color-code the garden piece, then answer the questions. Discuss: which reason has the strongest evidence?
Day 3: Assignment: Should Recess Be Longer? Students plan with the four-box planner, then draft.
Day 4: Revise the recess piece with a partner: circle each linking word, underline each example, and add one if a reason has none. Finish and submit.
Day 5: Assessment: Which Class Pet Should Room 12 Choose? Read the fact sheet aloud once; students plan and write on their own.

DIFFERENTIATION
- Support: provide the four-box planner with sentence starters ("I believe ___.", "One reason is ___. For example, ___.", "For these reasons, ___.").
- Support: let students dictate their plan before writing, and allow 100 words on the recess piece if needed.
- Stretch: add a counterargument ("Some people think ___, but ___.") and answer it.
- Multilingual learners: teach the linking words with gestures and examples, and let students plan orally with a same-language partner before writing in English.

FAMILY NOTE (send home at the start of the unit)
This week we are writing opinion pieces. Your child is learning to say what they think and then back it up with reasons and examples. At dinner, try a friendly debate: Which is better, summer or winter? Ask your child for two reasons and an example for each. Good reasons win the debate!",
  "id": "u2-teacher-guide",
  "purpose": "context",
  "title": "Teacher guide: Opinion Writing",
  "visibility": "teacher-only"
}
files.codex/u3-answer-key.json:
{
  "body": "Monarchs on the Move: Main Idea and Details: 1. Monarch butterflies make a very long migration each year, and it takes several generations to complete the round trip. 2. They glide on warm, rising air to save energy; they drink nectar for fuel and to store fat. 3. The fall monarchs that live up to eight months instead of two to six weeks; clues: \"special,\" \"can live for up to eight months,\" compared with \"most monarchs live only two to six weeks.\" 4. Females lay eggs on milkweed, and it is the only plant monarch caterpillars can eat. 5. The butterflies that fly north do not finish the trip; their children and grandchildren keep going until a later generation reaches the starting place. 6. Summaries should include the long journey to Mexico, how they manage it, the super generation, the generations that return north, and the threats and help.\nTwo Accounts of the Monarch Journey: Sourcing: the journal is by a girl who tagged a butterfly with her aunt; she was there (she uses I and me, describes holding the butterfly). The article is a secondhand account by a writer who gathered facts; it gives numbers and general facts and no personal experience. Context: the journal is from September 14, in a meadow behind a nature center, when monarchs begin flying south. The article tells the distance, the super generation, the winter in Mexico and the return over generations, which the girl could not see. The journal tells what tagging feels like, how to tell a male, and how the sticker works. Claim: either choice; strong answers explain the different focus (one butterfly and one day versus the whole migration) and use a detail from each.\nReading Check: Why Leaves Change Color: 1. Leaves change color in autumn because trees stop making chlorophyll, which lets other colors show, before the leaves drop for winter. 2. A pigment, or coloring, that leaves use to make food from sunlight; clues: \"a pigment, or coloring\" and \"make food from sunlight.\" 3. Trees stop making chlorophyll and it breaks down; the yellow and orange pigments were in the leaf all along and show when the green fades. 4. Sunny days and cool nights help some trees make more red pigment. 5. Example: shorter days and cooler nights (cause) make trees stop making chlorophyll (effect); or a layer of cells grows at the stem (cause) and the leaf drops (effect). 6. The summary names the green pigment, the fading in autumn, the yellow and red colors, and the leaf dropping.\nScoring tip: on the vocabulary criterion, a correct meaning without the clue words is Proficient; naming the clue words that gave the meaning is Advanced.",
  "id": "u3-answer-key",
  "purpose": "answer-key",
  "title": "Answer key: Reading to Learn",
  "visibility": "teacher-only"
}
files.codex/u3-overview.json:
{
  "body": "Informational texts teach us about the real world.

When you read to learn, ask:
- What is this text mostly about? That is the main idea.
- Which details explain or prove the main idea?
- What does a new word mean? Look at the words around it for clues.
- How is the text built? Does it tell events in order, explain causes and effects, or compare things?

In this unit we follow monarch butterflies on their long journey south. We will read an article by a writer who studied monarchs and a journal by a girl who held one in her hand, and we will compare what each one tells us.",
  "id": "u3-overview",
  "purpose": "context",
  "title": "Reading Like a Scientist",
  "visibility": "students"
}
files.codex/u3-teacher-guide.json:
{
  "body": "OBJECTIVES
- Students determine the main idea of a text, explain how key details support it, and summarize the text (RI.4.2).
- Students explain what happens and why in a scientific text, based on specific information in the text (RI.4.3).
- Students determine the meaning of domain-specific words and phrases using context clues (RI.4.4, L.4.4).
- Students describe the overall structure of a text, such as chronology or cause and effect (RI.4.5).
- Students compare a firsthand and a secondhand account of the same topic and describe the differences in focus and information (RI.4.6), referring to details in both (RI.4.1) and integrating information from two texts (RI.4.9).

MATERIALS
- "Monarchs on the Move" and "My Tagging Day" (in the activities), and "Why Leaves Change Color" (in the assessment)
- A world map, or a map of North America, to trace the migration route
- A two-column chart: Firsthand account / Secondhand account
- Optional: photos of monarchs, milkweed and tagged butterflies

FIVE-DAY PLAN
Day 1: Read Reading Like a Scientist. Show the migration route on a map. Model finding the main idea of one paragraph: cover the details, then ask what all of them are about.
Day 2: Lesson: Monarchs on the Move. Read aloud, then reread in pairs. Students answer the questions. Model the context clue for super generation together.
Day 3: Read "My Tagging Day." Fill the firsthand and secondhand chart as a class: who wrote it, were they there, what words show it, what each text focuses on.
Day 4: Assignment: Two Accounts of the Monarch Journey. Students answer the sourcing and context questions, then write their claim with a detail from each text.
Day 5: Assessment: Reading Check: Why Leaves Change Color. Students read on their own and answer in writing.

DIFFERENTIATION
- Support: give a main idea organizer (a table top with details as the legs). Pre-teach migration, generation, nectar, pigment and chlorophyll with pictures.
- Support: read the article aloud while students follow, and allow answers in phrases before full sentences.
- Stretch: ask which text structure each paragraph of "Monarchs on the Move" uses, and why the author might mix structures.
- Multilingual learners: many science words have cognates (migración, generación, clorofila, pigmento). Point them out, and pair students to retell each paragraph before writing.

FAMILY NOTE (send home at the start of the unit)
This week we are reading true texts about monarch butterflies, which fly up to 3,000 miles to spend the winter in Mexico. Your child is learning to find the main idea of a text and to compare an account by someone who was there with an account by someone who studied it. Ask your child: What surprised you about the monarchs? How did you learn it?",
  "id": "u3-teacher-guide",
  "purpose": "context",
  "title": "Teacher guide: Reading to Learn",
  "visibility": "teacher-only"
}
files.codex/u4-answer-key.json:
{
  "body": "Poet's Toolkit: \"Thunder Visits\": 1. Three stanzas, four lines each. 2. \"like a giant in a hurry\"; it compares thunder, loud and stomping, to a giant rushing down the hill. 3. Any two: \"comes stomping down the hill\" (stomping); \"rattles every windowsill\" (rattling); \"grumbles, yawns, and sighs\" (grumbling, yawning, sighing); \"wanders off to bed\" (going to bed). Also the clouds \"pull on their coats,\" the wind \"runs off to hide,\" the sun \"peeks out with sleepy eyes.\" 4. gray/bay and hide/side; the first and third lines rhyme and the second and fourth lines rhyme (ABAB). 5. The sound of rain tapping fast and steady, like fingers drumming on a table. 6. It starts loud and noisy (stomping, rattles, shakes) and ends calm and sleepy (yawns, sighs, sleepy eyes).\nPoem or Story? The Morning Bus: 1. The poem is in short lines, grouped into two stanzas, with a title; it does not use full sentences in every line. 2. The poem has a steady beat of about four strong beats, then three; the story has no regular beat. 3. cold/rolls (near rhyme), cloud/loud, aisle/mile, free/me; rhyme makes it musical and easy to remember. 4. Example: the bus doors: \"the bus doors opened with a hiss\" versus \"a hiss, a sigh, out loud.\" Also the time, the cold, the breath, the window seat. 5. A metaphor; her breath in the cold air looks like a small cloud. 6. Either; the answer gives an example from the chosen version.\nWhat the Poet Means: \"Grandpa's Hands\": The metaphor compares his hands to maps: the blue veins look like rivers and the wrinkles like roads, and like a map, the hands show everywhere they have been and everything they have done. Other examples: \"slow as Sunday\" (simile: slow and unhurried, like a quiet day off); \"they dance across the boat\" (personification: quick and graceful when fishing). Theme: a grandparent's hands carry a lifetime of work and love, and they will keep teaching the next generation; the map metaphor shows the past and the journey ahead.\nPoetry Check: \"The Old Oak in Winter\": 1. Three stanzas of four lines; pairs of lines rhyme (AABB: field/shield, deep/asleep, sky/by, ice/twice, door/more, see/tree). 2. A metaphor; the oak is strong, tough and refuses to give in, and its bark protects it like a shield. 3. Stubborn means refusing to give up or change; \"but the old oak never falls asleep\" and \"The wind pushes hard ... but\" show it will not give in. 4. \"Its branches are arms ... waving to geese\" (waving), \"It wears a white scarf of frost,\" or \"the squirrels say thank you.\" 5. \"like a friend at the door\"; spring returning is compared to a friend coming back, because it is welcome and familiar. 6. Theme: being patient and strong helps you get through hard times; supported by \"It has stood through a hundred winters\" and \"Being patient is part of being a tree.\"\nScoring tip: count \"the oak never falls asleep\" as personification too if the student explains it; a student who names the device but does not explain it is Developing on the figurative criterion.",
  "id": "u4-answer-key",
  "purpose": "answer-key",
  "title": "Answer key: Poems and Figurative Language",
  "visibility": "teacher-only"
}
files.codex/u4-overview.json:
{
  "body": "Poems are built differently from stories.

- A poem is written in lines, and groups of lines are called stanzas.
- Many poems have rhythm, a beat you can tap, and some have rhyme.
- Poets use figurative language to help us see things in a new way:
  a simile compares two things using like or as ("quiet as snow"),
  a metaphor says one thing is another ("the road is a ribbon"),
  personification gives human actions to something that is not human ("the wind whispered").

Read every poem at least twice, once out loud. Listen for the beat and picture what the words describe.",
  "id": "u4-overview",
  "purpose": "context",
  "title": "How Poems Work",
  "visibility": "students"
}
files.codex/u4-teacher-guide.json:
{
  "body": "OBJECTIVES
- Students explain major differences between poems and prose and refer to structural elements of poems: verse, rhythm, stanzas and rhyme (RL.4.5).
- Students explain similes, metaphors and personification in context (L.4.5).
- Students determine the meaning of words and phrases as used in a poem, including figurative language (RL.4.4).
- Students determine the theme of a poem from details in the text (RL.4.2).

MATERIALS
- "Thunder Visits," "The Morning Bus" (story and poem), "Grandpa's Hands" and "The Old Oak in Winter" (in the activities)
- A figurative language anchor chart: simile, metaphor, personification, each with an example
- Highlighters or colored pencils
- A drum or a desk to tap rhythm on

FIVE-DAY PLAN
Day 1: Read How Poems Work. Read "Thunder Visits" aloud twice while students tap the beat. Build the anchor chart with examples from the poem. Lesson: Poet's Toolkit.
Day 2: Assignment: Poem or Story? Students read both versions of "The Morning Bus" aloud with a partner, then answer. Discuss: what can a poem do that a paragraph cannot?
Day 3: Read "Grandpa's Hands" three times: for the picture, for the figurative language, for the feeling. Model explaining one metaphor out loud: what is compared, what they share, what it shows.
Day 4: Assignment: What the Poet Means. Students write about "Grandpa's Hands," then share with a partner who checks for a quoted line.
Day 5: Assessment: Poetry Check. Read "The Old Oak in Winter" aloud once; students reread and answer on their own.

DIFFERENTIATION
- Support: give a figurative language sort (cards with lines to sort into simile, metaphor and personification) before the assignment.
- Support: use a three-column frame for explaining figurative language: The poet compares ___ to ___. They are alike because ___. This shows ___.
- Stretch: students write their own four-line stanza about weather using a simile and personification.
- Multilingual learners: figurative language often does not translate word for word. Draw the literal picture ("hands that are maps") next to the meaning, and invite students to share a saying from their home language.

FAMILY NOTE (send home at the start of the unit)
We are reading poetry! Your child is learning words like stanza, simile ("as quiet as snow"), metaphor ("the road is a ribbon") and personification ("the wind whispered"). Try this game at home: look out the window and take turns describing the weather with a simile. "The clouds look like ___." You might hear some surprising poems.",
  "id": "u4-teacher-guide",
  "purpose": "context",
  "title": "Teacher guide: Poems and Figurative Language",
  "visibility": "teacher-only"
}
files.codex/u5-answer-key.json:
{
  "body": "Taking Notes Like a Researcher: 1. So they understand the idea, do not copy someone else's words, and can explain it themselves. 2. Example: \"weighs about a penny (Tiny Flyers)\". 3. Example: \"flapping uses lots of energy, so needs nectar from hundreds of flowers daily (Tiny Flyers)\". 4. It names the source, so the researcher can find the fact again and give credit. 5. Example: How far do hummingbirds migrate? What do hummingbirds do at night?\nSea Otter Research Notes: 1. thickest fur of any animal, up to about a million hairs per stamp-sized patch; air trapped in fur keeps water off skin; no blubber; groom for hours (Kelp); dirty fur makes them dangerously cold (Care Center). 2. eat about one quarter of body weight daily; crabs, clams, snails, sea urchins; crack shells on a rock on their chest (Kelp); fed clams and squid at the center (Care Center). 3. pups depend on mothers about six months; carried on mother's chest; mother grooms the fur; pup floats like a cork; wrapped in kelp while mother hunts (Care Center). 4. otters eat urchins; fewer urchins chew through kelp; kelp forests stay healthy for fish and other animals; keystone species (Kelp). 5. Example: how mothers raise pups, or how caretakers prepare a pup to return to the wild. 6. Example headings: Staying Warm, Finding Food, Raising Pups, Protecting the Kelp Forest.\nReport: All About Sea Otters: No single answer. An Advanced report introduces sea otters, has two or more sections with headings, uses facts from both texts (one from each at least), defines at least two topic words, uses linking words, ends with a conclusion and names both sources.\nScoring tip: copying long sentences from a text is Developing on the notes criterion even when the facts are correct; for the report, check development against both sources, not only the first.",
  "id": "u5-answer-key",
  "purpose": "answer-key",
  "title": "Answer key: Researching and Reporting",
  "visibility": "teacher-only"
}
files.codex/u5-overview.json:
{
  "body": "Researchers learn from more than one source and then teach what they learned.

Our research steps:
1. Ask a focus question: what do I want to find out?
2. Read each source and take notes in your own words, with only key words.
3. Write down where each note came from.
4. Sort your notes into categories. Each category becomes a section of your report.
5. Write the report: an introduction, sections with headings, facts and definitions, and a conclusion.

Our topic is the sea otter, an animal that floats on its back, uses rocks as tools, and protects an entire underwater forest.",
  "id": "u5-overview",
  "purpose": "context",
  "title": "Becoming a Researcher",
  "visibility": "students"
}
files.codex/u5-teacher-guide.json:
{
  "body": "OBJECTIVES
- Students gather relevant information from sources, take notes, categorize information and provide a list of sources (W.4.8).
- Students integrate information from two texts on the same topic in order to write knowledgeably (RI.4.9).
- Students conduct a short research project that builds knowledge of a topic (W.4.7).
- Students write an informative report that introduces a topic, groups related information in sections with headings, develops it with facts, definitions and details, uses linking words and precise vocabulary, and ends with a conclusion (W.4.2).

MATERIALS
- The note-taking passage (in the lesson) and "Sea Otters: Keepers of the Kelp" and "A Visit to the Otter Care Center" (in the activities)
- Index cards or a three-column note sheet with a Source column
- Colored markers for sorting notes by category
- A model report on a different animal, two short sections with headings

FIVE-DAY PLAN
Day 1: Read Becoming a Researcher. Lesson: Taking Notes Like a Researcher. Model "read, cover, write": read a sentence, cover it, write key words. Students practice with the hummingbird paragraph.
Day 2: Read "Sea Otters: Keepers of the Kelp" together. Students take notes with sources as they go. Discuss keystone species with the arch picture.
Day 3: Read "A Visit to the Otter Care Center." Assignment: Sea Otter Research Notes. Students finish their notes and sort them by color into three categories.
Day 4: Show the model report. Students turn each category into a section heading and plan their introduction and conclusion. Begin drafting.
Day 5: Assessment: Report: All About Sea Otters. Students write the report from their notes on their own (they may keep their notes and the texts).

DIFFERENTIATION
- Support: provide a note sheet with the questions printed as categories (Staying Warm, Food, Pups, Kelp Forests).
- Support: a report frame with the introduction sentence started and headings in place; a 150-word target.
- Stretch: add a text feature, such as a labeled diagram of the otter-urchin-kelp chain or a "Did you know?" box.
- Multilingual learners: build a word wall with pictures for kelp, urchin, blubber, groom and pup. Students may take notes in their home language and write the report in English.

FAMILY NOTE (send home at the start of the unit)
Our class is becoming researchers! We are reading two texts about sea otters, taking notes in our own words, and writing reports. Ask your child to teach you three things about sea otters, such as how they stay warm without blubber or why they are called keepers of the kelp. If your child is curious about another animal, a library book is a perfect next research project.",
  "id": "u5-teacher-guide",
  "purpose": "context",
  "title": "Teacher guide: Researching and Reporting",
  "visibility": "teacher-only"
}
files.codex/u6-answer-key.json:
{
  "body": "Chapter 1: Setting, Narrator and Characters: 1. The town of Millbrook, with a town clock stopped at 3:15 for twenty years; a tall, creaky new house with a dusty tower room; the present day, the family's first few days in town. 2. Ivy tells the story in first person; she uses I, me and we, and tells her own thoughts. 3. She is unhappy: she cares that she left her best friend, her old school and her \"whole life\" behind. 4. Tall, thin, gray beard, a frown that looks permanent; says \"Put that back where you found it\"; goes inside and shuts the door. 5. He recognizes the key and has feelings about it, maybe surprise, hope or sadness, that he quickly hides. 6. Predictions vary; a strong one connects 3:15 to the stopped clock.\nHow Mr. Okafor Changes: At first he is cold and unfriendly (frown, orders Ivy to put the key back, shuts the door). The library scene shows he was Mrs. Bell's helper and stopped the clock out of grief (Chapter 2). He changes when Ivy shows she understands and asks him to teach her; he explains a clock is \"a promise that tomorrow is coming,\" grins like in the photo, teaches her, and winds the clock with her every Sunday (Chapter 3). Lesson: sharing what we care about can help us heal, or new friends can help us move forward after a loss.\nThe Same Scene, Another Point of View: No single answer. Strong retellings use I and me as Mr. Okafor, keep the story's events and dialogue (\"Put that back where you found it,\" or \"She used to say a clock is a promise\"), and add his thoughts: recognizing Mrs. Bell's key, his grief, his surprise that Ivy knows, his hope when she asks to learn.\nWrite Your Own Story: A Found Object: No single answer. Score with the rubric: a clear character and situation at the start, dialogue punctuated with quotation marks, description of thoughts and feelings, events in order with transitions, and an ending that shows a change or lesson.\nScoring tip: for the point of view retelling, a scene told in third person (\"he thought\") instead of first person is Developing on the point of view criterion even when the events are accurate.",

- the setting: where and when the story happens,

{
  "body": "OBJECTIVES
- Students describe in depth a character, setting or event, drawing on specific details in the text (RL.4.3), and refer to details when explaining the text (RL.4.1).
- Students determine a theme from how a character changes (RL.4.2).
- Students compare the first-person and third-person points of view and retell a scene from another character's point of view (RL.4.6).
- Students write narratives with a clear situation, dialogue and description, a natural sequence with transitions, and a conclusion (W.4.3), organized for their audience (W.4.4), using correct capitalization, punctuation and quotation marks (L.4.2).

MATERIALS
- "The Clocktower Key," Chapters 1 to 3 (in the activities)
- A character chart: Says, Does, Thinks or feels, Others say about him, for Ivy and Mr. Okafor
- A story map planner: Character, Setting, Problem, Events, Solution
- A dialogue punctuation anchor chart: "Put that back," he said.

FIVE-DAY PLAN
Day 1: Read The Clocktower Key overview, then Chapter 1 aloud. Lesson: Chapter 1: Setting, Narrator and Characters. Start the character chart.
Day 2: Read Chapters 2 and 3, adding to the character chart after each one. Discuss: when did your feelings about Mr. Okafor change? Begin the assignment How Mr. Okafor Changes.
Day 3: Finish How Mr. Okafor Changes. Mini-lesson on point of view: retell one moment from Chapter 1 as a class in third person, then as Mr. Okafor in first person. Students start The Same Scene, Another Point of View.
Day 4: Finish the point of view retelling. Mini-lesson on dialogue punctuation. Students plan their own story on the story map.
Day 5: Assessment: Write Your Own Story: A Found Object. Students draft and revise on their own, then reread for quotation marks and transitions.

DIFFERENTIATION
- Support: read the chapters aloud while students follow, and provide the character chart partly filled in.
- Support: for the narrative, a story map with transition words printed beside each box; a 150-word target.
- Stretch: ask students to write a fourth chapter of "The Clocktower Key" that introduces a new problem, keeping Ivy's voice.
- Multilingual learners: preview each chapter with a picture walk and the key words (floorboard, brass, apprentice, gears). Allow the story plan to be drawn or written in the home language.

FAMILY NOTE (send home at the start of the unit)
This week we are reading "The Clocktower Key," a story about a girl who moves to a new town and finds a mysterious key. Then your child will write a story of their own. Ask your child: Who is Mr. Okafor, and why does he change? You might also share a story from your own life about something you found, or something you once lost. It may give your child an idea for their writing.",
  "id": "u6-teacher-guide",
  "purpose": "context",
  "title": "Teacher guide: Story Study: Characters and Narratives",
  "visibility": "teacher-only"
}
